title: Growth Models and Asymptotes
objectives: Contrast linear, exponential and logarithmic growth and match each to a described scenario
Compute doubling time exactly and with the rule of 70
Identify vertical and horizontal asymptotes of rational, logarithmic, exponential and saturation models
Evaluate compound-interest balances under annual, periodic and continuous compounding
Evaluate a saturation model $L(1-e^{-kt})$ at a given time and interpret its asymptote
motivation: A portfolio that compounds at 8% per year, a market-data feed that fills a buffer at a steady rate, and a new exchange that saturates as adoption approaches its capacity ceiling all grow, but at fundamentally different speeds, and confusing them leads to absurd forecasts. Choosing the right growth model, and knowing where it can never go (its asymptotes), is the difference between a defensible projection and fiction. This lesson builds the vocabulary you will reuse in every quantitative model that follows.

blocks.md: **Linear growth** adds a fixed amount per step: $y = mx + b$. Add $100 per year and after 10 years you have added exactly $1{,}000. **Exponential growth** multiplies by a fixed factor per step: $y = a \cdot b^x$ with $b > 1$. Add 8% per year and the *increments themselves grow*, because each year's interest earns interest. **Logarithmic growth** is the mirror image: $y = \ln x$ rises fast at first and then flattens, yet never stops climbing, it is unbounded, just painfully slow.

blocks.caption: On $0 \le x \le 8$: the line $y = 0.5x$, exponential $y = 2^x$ and logarithmic $y = \log_2 x$. Notice how $2^x$ and $\log_2 x$ hug the line early on, then diverge in opposite directions.

blocks.md: A concrete logarithmic example from computing: binary search over a sorted collection of $n$ records costs about $\log_2 n$ probes. One million records need about 20 probes because $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ - and doubling the dataset adds just **one** more probe. That sluggishness is why logarithmic cost is the gold standard for lookup-heavy trading systems.

blocks.text: Doubling time and the rule of 70

blocks.md: For exponential growth $A(t) = A_0 e^{rt}$ (with $r$ the continuous rate), doubling means $e^{rt} = 2$, so $t = \ln 2 / r \approx 0.693 / r$. Multiplying numerator and denominator by 100 gives the handy **rule of 70**: doubling time in years is roughly $70$ divided by the growth rate in percent.

blocks.title: Worked example: doubling at 7% per year
items: The three answers differ by at most a few percent, fine for intuition, not for valuation.

blocks.text: Compound interest and the emergence of $e$

blocks.md: Compounding $n$ times per year for one year at nominal rate $r$ turns \$1 into $(1 + r/n)^n$. Watch what happens as the compounding frequency grows, at $r = 8\%$:

The effective rate climbs toward a **ceiling**: $(1 + r/n)^n \to e^r$ as $n \to \infty$, giving $e^{0.08} - 1 = 8.3287\%$. That ceiling is a **horizontal asymptote** of the effective-rate function. Going from daily to continuous compounding adds under one basis point, a fact desks exploit when quoting 'continuous' rates that are really just a convention.

blocks.caption: Growth of \$1{,}000 at 8% per year. Each decade roughly doubles the balance, exponential growth is multiplicative, not additive.

blocks.md: Over 5 years the balance reaches $1000 \times 1.08^5 = $1{,}469.33$; over 30 years it reaches $1000 \times 1.08^{30} \approx $10{,}062.66$. Ten times the time, ten times the multiple of principal, that is the signature of a constant exponential rate.

blocks.text: Asymptotes: lines a graph can approach but not cross

blocks.md: A **vertical asymptote** is a value of $x$ where the function blows up: $y = 1/x$ and $y = \ln x$ both explode as $x \to 0^+$. A **horizontal asymptote** is a value of $y$ the function settles toward as $x \to \infty$: $y = e^{-x}$ decays to $0$, and $1/x \to 0$ as well. Asymptotes are not decoration, they encode hard limits of a model.

blocks.title: A perpetuity has a vertical asymptote
blocks.md: A perpetuity paying \$5 per year forever is worth $\text{PV} = 5/y$ at discount rate $y$. At $y = 4\%$ it is worth \$125; at $y = 1\%$ it is worth \$500; as $y \to 0^+$ the value explodes. The line $y = 0$ is a vertical asymptote, the mathematics behind 'bond prices go haywire near zero rates'.

blocks.text: Saturation models: growth with a ceiling

blocks.md: Real growth often hits capacity: market share cannot exceed 100%, a user base cannot exceed the population. A simple saturation model is $N(t) = L\,(1 - e^{-kt})$, which starts growing at rate $kL$ and flattens toward the **carrying capacity** $L$ - its horizontal asymptote. The whole model lives between $0$ and $L$; it can never overshoot.

blocks.title: Worked example: adoption approaching capacity
items: At $t = 10$: $e^{-4} = 0.0183$, so $N(10) = 19{,}637$ - already within 2% of the ceiling.
Doubling the time does not double adoption: growth is decelerating toward the asymptote $N = 20000$.

blocks.title: Logarithmic growth is unbounded: just slow
blocks.md: Students often think $\ln x$ 'levels off' to a horizontal asymptote. It does not: $\ln x$ eventually exceeds every fixed number, no matter how large. It merely grows more slowly than any positive power of $x$. Unbounded-but-slow and bounded are different claims, confusing them misprices models with hard capacity limits.

guidedExercise.prompt: A fund projects its assets under management as $A(t) = 50\,000\,e^{0.06t}$ (dollars, $t$ in years). (a) Estimate the doubling time with the rule of 70, then compute it exactly. (b) Compute $A(12)$ to the nearest hundred dollars. (c) State the horizontal asymptote and interpret it, or explain why none exists.
hints: Doubling needs $e^{0.06t} = 2$; take logs of both sides.
Rule of 70: divide 70 by the rate in percent.
$e^{0.06t} \to \infty$, so ask what horizontal limits a growing exponential can have.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) Rule of 70: $70/6 \approx 11.7$ years. Exactly: $t = \ln 2 / 0.06 = 0.6931/0.06 \approx 11.55$ years. (b) $A(12) = 50\,000 \, e^{0.72} = 50\,000 \times 2.0544 \approx $102{,}700$. (c) There is **no** horizontal asymptote: $A(t) \to \infty$. Unbounded growth models have none above; asymptotes belong to models with ceilings ($N(t) = L(1-e^{-kt}) \to L$) or decay ($e^{-x} \to 0$).

independentExercise.prompt: An options desk rolls out a new pricing service to 4,500 trading accounts. Adoption follows $N(t) = 4500\,(1 - e^{-0.5t})$, with $t$ in weeks. (a) How many accounts are onboarded after 2 weeks? (b) After 6 weeks? (c) The desk's infrastructure handles 4,200 accounts; by trial, find the first whole week $t$ at which $N(t)$ exceeds that capacity.
hints: $e^{-1} = 0.3679$, $e^{-3} = 0.0498$ - you can evaluate (a) and (b) without a calculator.
For (c), try $t = 6, 7, 8, \dots$ and watch $N(t)$ climb toward 4500.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $N(2) = 4500(1 - e^{-1}) = 4500 \times 0.6321 = 2{,}844$. (b) $N(6) = 4500(1 - e^{-3}) = 4500 \times 0.9502 = 4{,}276$. (c) Since $4{,}276 > 4{,}200$ at $t = 6$, check earlier weeks: $N(5) = 4500(1 - e^{-2.5}) = 4500 \times 0.9179 = 4{,}131 \le 4{,}200$. **Capacity is first breached at week 6.** The asymptote $L = 4500$ sits just above the limit, so the desk must expand infrastructure before the curve finishes flattening.

commonMistakes: Treating percentage growth as additive: 8% per year for 5 years multiplies by $1.08^5 \approx 1.47$, not by $1 + 5 \times 0.08$.
Claiming $\ln x$ has a horizontal asymptote, it is unbounded, only slow.
Mixing the rule of 70 with continuous compounding answers and expecting exact agreement; it is an approximation to $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$.
Reading a saturation model's ceiling $L$ as something the curve can overshoot; $1 - e^{-kt} < 1$ always.
realWorldApplication: Infrastructure capacity planning is applied growth modelling: user sign-ups follow saturation curves toward a ceiling, storage grows linearly, and compute demand for naive algorithms grows exponentially, each needs a different forecast and a different budget.
quantFinanceApplication: Doubling time and the rule of 70 give traders instant intuition for compounding returns; continuous compounding $e^{rt}$ is the standard discounting convention; and saturation models describe market-share ceilings and the flattening of adoption curves for new venues and products.
summary: Linear growth adds, exponential growth multiplies ($y = ab^x$), logarithmic growth is unbounded but slower than any positive power.
Doubling time: $t = \ln 2/r$ exactly, or about $70/\text{rate\%}$ by the rule of 70.
Compounding more frequently lifts the effective rate toward the horizontal asymptote $e^r - 1$: at 8% nominal, from 8.000% (annual) to 8.329% (continuous).
Vertical asymptotes mark values where a model blows up (e.g. perpetuity value $5/y$ as $y \to 0^+$); horizontal asymptotes mark ceilings or floors (saturation $L(1-e^{-kt}) \to L$).

quiz.prompt: Which function has $y = 0$ as a horizontal asymptote as $x \to \infty$?
quiz.explanation: $e^{-x} \to 0$ from above. $2^x$ and $x^3$ diverge to infinity, and $\ln x$ grows without bound (just slowly).

quiz.prompt: Using the rule of 70, estimate the doubling time in years for money growing at 5% per year.
quiz.explanation: $70/5 = 14$ years. The exact continuously-compounded answer is $\ln 2/0.05 \approx 13.86$, so the rule is close.

quiz.prompt: \$1,000 is invested at 8% compounded annually for 5 years. What is the balance, to the nearest cent?
quiz.explanation: $1000 \times 1.08^5 = 1000 \times 1.469328 = $1{,}469.33$. Exponential growth multiplies the principal by the factor $1.08^5$.

quiz.prompt: Select every true statement about logarithmic growth $y = \ln x$.
options: It eventually grows more slowly than $x^{0.1}$
quiz.explanation: $\ln x$ exceeds any fixed value eventually (unbounded) but any positive power of $x$ outgrows it; its domain is $x > 0$. It has **no** horizontal asymptote, the flattening never settles to a limit.

quiz.prompt: A product's adoption follows $N(t) = 20000\,(1 - e^{-0.4t})$. What is $N(5)$, to the nearest whole user?
quiz.explanation: $e^{-0.4 \times 5} = e^{-2} = 0.1353$, so $N(5) = 20000 \times 0.8647 = 17{,}293$ - approaching, but never reaching, the ceiling $L = 20000$.

quiz.prompt: In one or two sentences: why does the rule of 70 work? Name the constant it approximates.
quiz.modelAnswer: Doubling time is $t = \ln 2 / r$; since $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$, multiplying numerator and denominator by 100 gives $t \approx 70/\text{rate\%}$ - the rule of 70 approximates $100\ln 2 \approx 69.3$ with the rounder number 70.
quiz.explanation: The rule is a disguised form of $t = \ln 2/r$, using $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$ rounded up to 0.70.

flashcards.back: A line $y = c$ that the graph approaches as $x \to \pm\infty$ without reaching: $e^{-x} \to 0$, saturation $L(1-e^{-kt}) \to L$, effective compounding rate $\to e^r - 1$.
$(1 + r/n)^n \to e^r$ as the compounding frequency $n \to \infty$: continuous compounding is the limit of ever-faster discrete compounding.
$N(t) = L(1 - e^{-kt})$ - starts at $0$, initial growth rate $kL$, horizontal asymptote $N = L$ (carrying capacity).
$\ln x$ is unbounded but grows slower than any $x^p$, $p > 0$. Bounded models (saturation) flatten to a limit. 'Flattening' does not imply a ceiling.
